---

Forgive me—this is not that poem
of raised garden beds, blossoming borders,
peonies, gardenias, poinsettias,
a golden orb ascending slow
over an endless amber landscape—
cardinals darting through open air,
thrushes, sparrows,
blue skies scented with lavender
washing the mind toward virtue.

If only I could paint language
in pastels upon a canvas of thistledown—
but deceit comes to mind instead:
a lie. A betrayer. A turncoat. A recreant.
Backstabber to truth,
I would be gutted a thousand times over.

This is not that poem,
nor am I that poet—
to hold your hand
.or. silence the screams from knot-holes,
blood upon a cement floor,
.or. call suicide another form of escape.
No—no—no.

But I do bear witness:
the ugliness humans inflict upon one another,
upon their own [selves],
how time becomes malice, becomes death,
igniting the eyes with a spite
inextinguishable, once unleashed—

Forgive state poet #289–128
for refusing to scribble illusions of artifice,
as if an eternal hell
could ever be contained
by stanza,
by alliteration,
by slant rhyme—

---

I preserved the fragmented punctuation (.or.), the bracketed [selves], the numbered designation, and the triple negation ("no-no-no") as these appear to be deliberate stylistic choices central to the poem's rawness and voice. Let me know if you'd like adjustments to tone, rhythm, or specific phrasing.

outputs.L3:
# The Refusal

I will not write you a poem about flowers today.
There will be no birdsong here, no meadows
soft with morning light, no pastoral scene
where lambs graze beneath forgiving skies.
I call attention to this absence deliberately—
the poem you expected is not the poem you will receive.

To craft such beauty now, to weave together
petals and dew and the gentle music of wrens,
would be a kind of lying. It would be deceit
dressed in the finest language, comfort purchased
at the cost of honesty. I refuse to be
a traitor to truth, even when truth is unbearable,
even when the world begs for something softer.

I cannot hold your hand through this.
I cannot smooth over the wreckage,
cannot erase the violence that echoes
through histories both personal and vast,
cannot pretend the trauma isn't real,
cannot look away from the suicides,
the quiet rooms where someone chose
to stop existing rather than continue.
These things happened. They are happening still.
I will not paper over them with verse.

But I promise you this much:
I will name the evil when I see it.
I will acknowledge the malice
humans visit upon each other—
and upon themselves, in private,
in the dark hours when no one is watching.
This much I owe you. This much is true.

I am state poet #289-128,
and I ask your forgiveness now—
not for what I will say,
but for what I will withhold.
I will not use alliteration to soften horror.
I will not let rhyme's sweet symmetry
disguise the jagged edges of what is real.
I will not aestheticize this hell
into something palatable, something
that fits neatly into anthologies
of human suffering made beautiful.

The truth is timeless and it is not kind.
I only ask that you let me tell it plainly,
without the flowers,
without the birdsong,
without the lie of beauty
where beauty does not belong.
outputs.L4:
# On the Refusal of Beauty: An Exploration of Poetic Honesty in the Face of Violence

This poem stages a fundamental crisis of representation—one that many poets who write about atrocity, trauma, or human cruelty have confronted. At its core, the poem enacts a refusal: the speaker will not write the poem that convention, and perhaps readers, might expect or even desire. That expected poem would be filled with the traditional furniture of "nice" poetry—flowers nodding in gentle breezes, birdsong threading through morning light, soft pastel washes of color meant to soothe and please. This is the poetry of greeting cards, of pastoral tradition stretching back through centuries of verse that finds in nature a mirror for human tranquility and grace.

But the speaker cannot, in good conscience, write this poem. To do so would constitute a betrayal—not merely an aesthetic failure but a moral one. The poem's true subject matter is unbearable: violence that leaves marks on bodies and minds, screams that tear through silence, blood that stains the literal and metaphorical ground, suicide as the devastating terminus of human suffering. These are not natural phenomena like storms or droughts; they are evils that human beings inflict upon one another and, in the case of suicide, upon themselves as a response to unbearable pain. To wrap such realities in the gauze of pastoral beauty would be to lie about their nature, to aestheticize what should horrify, to make palatable what must remain difficult.

The poem's significance emerges precisely from this refusal. The speaker will not employ alliteration's musical repetition to soften harsh consonants of violence into something that trips pleasantly off the tongue. The speaker will not reach for slant rhyme's clever near-misses, those poetic techniques that create satisfying patterns of sound, because such patterns risk transforming suffering into craft, into something to be admired for its formal ingenuity rather than confronted in its raw truth. Every technique of beautification becomes, in this context, a technique of concealment—a way of making bearable what the speaker insists must remain unbearable if it is to be honestly witnessed.

This constitutes an ethics of poetic form as much as content. The poem argues, implicitly and explicitly, that authentic witness to human suffering demands the sacrifice of conventional aesthetic pleasure. Beauty becomes suspect precisely because of its power to console, to distance, to transform horror into something contemplatable, even enjoyable, in its expression. The speaker chooses instead a kind of formal austerity or roughness that mirrors the ugliness of the subject matter—asserting that how we say something about violence matters as much as what we say, and that dishonesty of form is itself a species of moral failure.

In this way, the poem becomes a meditation on the responsibilities of the witness-poet: to resist the seductions of craft when craft would falsify, to choose fidelity to painful truth over the comforts of literary beauty, and to insist that some realities demand to be rendered starkly, without ornament, if they are to be honored rather than betrayed.
outputs.L5:
# Sorry, This...

There's a peculiar power in the phrase "sorry, this." It hangs there, incomplete, bracing for whatever follows. Sorry, this seat is taken. Sorry, this isn't working out. Sorry, this is going to hurt a little.

We use these three words as a cushion before delivering something unwelcome. The apology arrives first, softening the blow before we even know what the blow will be. It's almost reflexive—a linguistic habit born from politeness, awkwardness, or genuine regret.

Think about how often you've heard it, or said it yourself. A barista explaining sorry, this machine is down. A doctor beginning sorry, this may sting. A friend texting sorry, this is going to sound harsh, but... Each instance carries its own weight, yet they all share that same preemptive wince, that same attempt to soften what's coming.

There's something very human about needing to apologize before we've even said the thing we're apologizing for. It suggests an awareness of impact, a small act of empathy extended toward the person about to receive news, criticism, or inconvenience. We know words can sting, disappoint, or complicate things, so we reach for "sorry" like a handrail.

But the phrase can also become a crutch. When overused, "sorry, this" loses its sincerity, turning into filler rather than genuine acknowledgment. It can undercut confidence—apologizing for taking up space, for having an opinion, for existing in a way that might inconvenience someone else.

Perhaps the real skill lies in knowing when the phrase is warranted. Sorry, this coffee is cold—yes, worth saying. Sorry, this idea I have might be brilliant—perhaps not. Language shapes how we carry ourselves through the world, and three small words, repeated enough times, can either build bridges of consideration or chip away at our own sense of worth.

So the next time "sorry, this" rises to your lips, it might be worth pausing—not to suppress it entirely, but to ask whether it's an act of grace, or simply a habit worth breaking.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poem from the perspective of an incarcerated person who refuses to write the pretty nature poem they were asked for, and instead confronts the darker truths of prison life.
counterfactuals.output:
# What You Asked For

You wanted birds.
You wanted me to write about birds,
maybe a tree, something with roots
that still remembers dirt,
some light coming through
a window I don't have.

I don't have a window.
I have a slot in a door
where a hand pushes a tray twice a day,
and if that's a metaphor for anything
it's not the kind you can hang
in a gallery with a little card
that says *resilience*.

You want me to transcend this.
I want to tell you what the walls sound like
at 3 a.m. when someone is screaming
for a mother who's been dead six years
and nobody comes,
because coming doesn't fix anything,
coming is just paperwork
that gets filed under *incident*.

I could give you a metaphor for a caged bird.
Everyone gives you a metaphor for a caged bird.
But I am not a bird. Birds get to leave.
I am a man with a number sewn into his shirt
where his name should sit,
and the state has decided
that number is truer than what my mother called me.

So no—no poem about seasons changing,
no poem about hope like a green shoot
pushing through concrete,
because concrete doesn't crack for hope,
it cracks from freeze and thaw and time,
the same as I'm cracking,
not blooming, cracking,
and there's a difference
you'd know if you were in here.

I'll tell you what's true instead:
the fluorescent lights don't turn off, not fully,
they hum a low dim all night
so even my dreams have a witness,
even my dreams are surveilled.

I'll tell you about the man three cells down
who found God two years ago
and still can't sleep without the light on
because the dark, in here, has teeth.

I'll tell you the commissary raised prices on soap
the same month they cut the visit hours,
like they want us dirty and unseen,
like clean and visible
are privileges, not rights.

You wanted a nature poem.
Here's your nature:
we are animals in enclosures
built by other animals
who sleep fine at night
because they've never had to learn
what their own name sounds like
when no one's said it in a year.

That's the only truth I've got today.
No birds.
Just this.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a free-verse piece titled with a prisoner ID number that rejects flowery imagery (peonies, gardenias) in favor of raw honesty about violence and despair.
counterfactuals.output:
# 47291-B

I will not tell you the peonies bloomed
outside my window that morning,
because there is no window,
and even if there were,
nothing blooms here except bruises,
purple then yellow then gone,
the way everything here
learns to disappear.

I will not compare her scream
to gardenias wilting in heat,
because a scream is just a scream,
ugly and true,
tearing out of a throat
like something that was never
meant to stay quiet.

Let me say instead:
the concrete floor is cold at 3 AM.
The guards change shifts and forget your name
faster than you forgot the sun.
Someone down the hall is crying
and it doesn't sound like rain
or violins or anything
a poet would want to write about.

It sounds like a man
who has run out
of reasons.

I've stopped looking for beauty
in the rust stains on the ceiling,
stopped pretending the cough
in the next cell
is anything but a body
breaking down slow,
no metaphor required.

They took his shoelaces.
They took the mirror.
They took the word "someday"
and replaced it with a number
I now answer to
more than my own name.

This is not a poem about survival
as some triumphant thing,
some phoenix rising.
This is a poem about a Tuesday,
then another Tuesday,
then a hundred more
that all taste like the same
metal spoon,
the same fluorescent hum,
the same fear
that doesn't need
a single flower
to make it real.

I am not a wilting rose.
I am a man
counting cinderblocks,
learning the exact weight
of a door that only opens
from the outside.

That's the whole poem.
No garden. No grace.
Just this—
the truth,
unadorned,
still standing.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poem that starts by describing a beautiful garden scene, then pivots into an anti-poem about lies, self-harm, and human cruelty, ending with a refusal to romanticize suffering through poetic devices like alliteration or rhyme.
counterfactuals.output:
# Garden

The roses open slow as breath,
gold light spills across the grass,
a bee drifts drunk through honeysuckle,
and everything here agrees to be beautiful
because I have asked it to.

That's the lie.

I wanted to write you a garden
so I could avoid writing the other thing—
the fist, the silence after,
the mirror someone stood before
too long, deciding what to carve
into their own skin like it was
the only language left that told the truth.

I could rhyme it. I could dress the wound
in soft consonants, let alliteration
lull you—*bruised, blooming, breaking, beautiful*—
stack the words like stones
across a grave until it looks
like landscaping.

I won't do that.

Cruelty doesn't scan.
It doesn't want your couplets.
The man who hurts what's smaller than him
doesn't care that you found
an elegant enjambment for his violence.
The girl who hates her body
in the dark isn't comforted
by assonance.

So here it is, plain:
people lie to each other constantly,
and to themselves worse.
People hurt themselves quietly
in rooms you'll never see.
People are cruel not in some
grand operatic way but small,
repeated, daily—
a word chosen to wound,
a door closed on purpose,
a silence held like a weapon.

I won't rhyme any of that.
I won't make the hurting pretty
so it goes down easier.
Some things don't get a garden.
Some things just are
what they are—
ugly,
unmetered,
true.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a dark, experimental poem where the speaker apologizes for not delivering the peaceful, natural imagery expected of them, instead exposing themes of betrayal, incarceration, and inescapable inner turmoil.
counterfactuals.output:
# What You Wanted Instead of This

I promised you a field.
I promised you the way light
breaks itself gently on water,
how a bird might carry
the whole weight of morning
in one small throat.

I'm sorry. That poem died
in a room I can't describe to you—
concrete learning the shape
of a body that stopped
believing in doors.

You wanted moss.
You wanted the soft
architecture of moths
against a porch light,
something that forgives you
just by existing.

Instead: here is a hand
that isn't mine anymore,
counting hours by the sound
of keys that don't belong
to any lock I know.

Here is the friend
who became a hallway.
Here is the word *safe*
turning its back slowly,
walking into another
person's mouth.

I know you wanted the ocean.
I know you wanted its blue
uncomplicated hunger,
the way it takes everything
and calls it *communion*.

But there is no tide here—
only the same four corners
learning my name
better than I do,
only the static hour
that repeats itself
like a warden checking a cell
that was never empty
to begin with.

I'm sorry for the absence
of anything that grows.
I'm sorry the field
became a courtyard,
the bird became an alarm,
the light became
the thing that finds you
even when you've learned
to disappear.

This is not the poem
you wanted.

This is the one
that survived.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4
